Data Attribution at Scale via Influence Matrix Estimation

Yuxi Chen Affiliation: Department of Statistics & Data Science    Hamza Golubovic Affiliation: Department of Statistics Email: hg2723@columbia.edu    Han Tong Affiliation: Department of Statistics Email: ht2672@columbia.edu    Arian Maleki Affiliation: Department of Statistics Affiliation: Electrical Engineering Department Email: mm4338@columbia.edu    Andrew IlyasCarnegie Mellon University Email: {ericc3, andrewi}@andrew.cmu.eduColumbia University Affiliation: Software and Societal Systems Department Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
September 14, 2026
Abstract

Data attribution seeks to quantify how individual training examples shape a model’s predictions and underpins problems including data valuation, machine unlearning, and model interpretability. Despite having a long line of work, computationally scalable methods often struggle to predict the effect of removing training data in neural networks due to their non-convex nature. To overcome this challenge, metagradient-based methods such as MAGIC (Ilyas and Engstrom, 2025) differentiate each prediction through the entire training run and compute its exact influence with respect to the training data, but require a separate run for every prediction. To reduce this cost, we cast budgeted attribution as estimating a large influence matrix from a small number of measurements. We show that the measurements most appropriate for recovering this matrix differ from those best suited for attribution itself. We then present two algorithms, Mage and Spell, suited for reconstruction and attribution respectively, that run on existing metagradient machinery at no extra cost. Empirical studies demonstrate strong performance over existing baselines across training scales and measurement budgets.

1 Introduction

With the success of modern deep learning, understanding how training data shapes model behavior has become increasingly important. Previous studies have traced many undesirable model behaviors back to the training data, showing that neural networks can memorize private records (Carlini et al., 2021), inherit targeted vulnerabilities from a few poisoned examples (Wan et al., 2023), and learn shortcuts by relying on signals that are predictive yet brittle (Ilyas et al., 2019). At the same time, data selection allows smaller datasets to match or surpass the performance of larger counterparts for vision and language model training (Sorscher et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024). Similar effects likewise appear during post-training, where a curated fraction of the data can elicit strong instruction following and reasoning (Zhou et al., 2023; Xia et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025). Together, these findings testify to the central role of training data in shaping model behavior.

One way to understand the impact of training data is to ask how a given metric of interest (e.g., held-out test loss) would have changed had the same model been trained on a different dataset. To answer this question naively would require one to modify the training dataset, retrain the new model, and observe the resulting outputs. Instead, predictive data attribution seeks to predict this counterfactual quantity without retraining (Ilyas et al., 2022) by estimating the contribution of every training example to the prediction of interest. Previous works have studied this problem using tools like approximate influence functions (Koh and Liang, 2017), Shapley values (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019), trajectory tracing (Pruthi et al., 2020), and scalable approximations of influence functions (Park et al., 2023). Despite their computational appeal, these methods have often produced estimates that align poorly with the true outcome of retraining in neural networks (Bae et al., 2022; Bae et al., 2024).

Overcoming these hurdles, MAGIC (Ilyas and Engstrom, 2025) differentiates the loss from a test prediction backward through the entire optimization trajectory, computing its gradient with respect to the training data weights. This gradient—also known as the exact influence function—near-perfectly predicts the effects of modifying the training dataset on the given test prediction’s loss. However, computing the exact influence function with MAGIC would require a separate reverse differentiation through the full training run for every prediction of interest. This makes MAGIC expensive to scale to settings where we wish to study many held-out examples individually.

In this work, we ask whether the cost of data attribution can be reduced when estimating the influence scores across many predictions. Our contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We cast the problem of budgeted data attribution across many predictions as that of estimating a Jacobian matrix of influence scores from a limited number of left and right vector products.

  2. 2.

    We formalize two distinct objectives, reconstruction and attribution, and show that the two are optimized using different measurements, since reconstruction weights each prediction by its squared row norm whereas attribution weights them equally.

  3. 3.

    We introduce Mage (Metagradient Approximation by Gram Eigendirections) for reconstruction and Spell (SPherical Estimation for the Linear datamodeling score at Low budgets) for attribution, both of which run on existing metagradient machinery.

  4. 4.

    Across a ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10 and a 92M-parameter language model on TinyStories, Mage and Spell each outperform existing computable alternatives on their intended objective under various measurement budgets.

2 Predictive Data Attribution and Influence Matrix Estimation

We begin by formalizing both the predictive data attribution framework and the underlying computational primitives. The central idea is to parameterize the training dataset through continuous importance weights, after which our goal becomes computing derivatives of the trained model behavior with respect to these weights. Finally, we state the problem of estimating the influence matrix under a limited budget and define two objectives, reconstruction and attribution, which emphasize distinct aspects of any estimate.

2.1 Setup and Notation

We follow the datamodeling framework of Ilyas et al. (2022). Let 𝒟={xi}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} be a dataset of nn training points. We parameterize the training set by an importance-weight vector w∈ℝnw\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, where wiw_{i} scales the contribution of example ii to the training loss. With this representation, a standard training pipeline corresponds to w=𝟏nw=\mathbf{1}_{n}, where 𝟏n∈ℝn\mathbf{1}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the all-ones vector, and setting wi=0w_{i}=0 amounts to removing example ii from the training set.

Next, let Θ⊆ℝp\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} denote the parameter space and let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a learning algorithm mapping data weights to trained model parameters,

𝒜:ℝn→Θ,θ⁡(w)=𝒜⁡(w).\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\Theta,\qquad\theta(w)=\mathcal{A}(w).

The learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} encompasses every aspect of training beyond the data weights, including the model architecture, optimizer, and learning rate schedule.

Following the single-model setting of Ilyas and Engstrom (2025), we also fix every source of training randomness, whereby the same weighting ww always generates the same parameters θ⁡(w)\theta(w). We further assume that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is iterative and smooth, meaning that θ⁡(w)\theta(w) is produced by a fixed sequence of differentiable training updates, and small perturbations to ww produce controlled changes in the resulting model output and its derivative.

Finally, we are given kk test queries that we wish to attribute to the training data. Throughout, we write [k]={1,…,k}[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}. For each test query q∈[k]q\in[k], we let ϕq:Θ→ℝ\phi_{q}:\Theta\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a differentiable scalar measurement of the trained model (e.g., the loss of the model with parameters θ\theta on test query qq). We define the model output function fqf_{q}

fq​(w)=ϕq​(θ⁡(w))=ϕq​(𝒜⁡(w))f_{q}(w)=\phi_{q}(\theta(w))=\phi_{q}(\mathcal{A}(w)) (1)

as the composition function mapping data weights directly to the measurement for query qq, so that fq​(w)f_{q}(w) is the value that would be observed on query qq if the model were trained using data weights ww. We collect these functions into the vector-valued model output function FF,

F⁡(w)=(f1​(w),…,fk​(w))∈ℝk.F(w)=\left(f_{1}(w),\ldots,f_{k}(w)\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{k}.

At a high level, our goal is to return an estimate F^=(f^1,…,f^k)\widehat{F}=(\widehat{f}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{f}_{k}) of this function, which predicts the model behavior under any weighting ww without retraining.

2.2 Metagradients and MAGIC

The composition in Equation 1 makes the model output function fq​(w)f_{q}(w) differentiable with respect to the training weights, and its derivative

∇wfq​(𝟏n)=∇wϕq​(𝒜⁡(w))|w=𝟏n∈ℝn\nabla_{w}f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})=\nabla_{w}\,\phi_{q}(\mathcal{A}(w))\big|_{w=\mathbf{1}_{n}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

is called the metagradient of query qq, a gradient taken through the entire training procedure. Its iith entry measures how the observed value on query qq would respond to an infinitesimal change in the weight of training example ii. Since computing this derivative naively would be computationally prohibitive, Engstrom et al. (2025) introduce REPLAY, which computes metagradients for large-scale training runs at a cost comparable to that of training itself. Hereinafter, we use the word “replay” synonymously with the REPLAY algorithm.

To leverage metagradients for data attribution, MAGIC (Ilyas and Engstrom, 2025) linearizes the model output function fqf_{q} around w=𝟏nw=\mathbf{1}_{n} with a first-order Taylor expansion,

fq​(w)≈f^q​(w)=fq​(𝟏n)+⟨∇wfq​(𝟏n),w−𝟏n⟩,f_{q}(w)\approx\widehat{f}_{q}(w)=f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})+\langle\nabla_{w}f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}),\,w-\mathbf{1}_{n}\rangle,

which defines a linear predictor for studying the effect of removing any subset of training examples. Let S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] be a subset of examples to remove and let 𝟏S∈{0,1}n\mathbf{1}_{S}\in\{0,1\}^{n} be its indicator vector, so that training without the examples in SS corresponds to the weighting 𝟏n−𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{S}. Writing Δq​(S)\Delta_{q}(S) for the resulting change in query qq, MAGIC predicts

Δq(S)=fq(𝟏n−𝟏S)−fq(𝟏n)≈−⟨∇wfq(𝟏n), 1S⟩=−∑i∈S[∇wfq(𝟏n)]i.\Delta_{q}(S)=f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{S})-f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})\approx-\left\langle\nabla_{w}f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}),\,\mathbf{1}_{S}\right\rangle=-\sum_{i\in S}\left[\nabla_{w}f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})\right]_{i}.

Since the metagradient is evaluated at 𝟏n\mathbf{1}_{n} and does not depend on 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S}, a single metagradient allows us to generate counterfactual predictions for all subsets of 𝒟\mathcal{D} simultaneously, and these predictions have been shown to near-perfectly estimate the effects of removing training data (Ilyas and Engstrom, 2025).

Finally, we collect the metagradients across all kk queries and define the influence matrix

Y=∂F⁡(w)∂w|w=𝟏n∈ℝk×n,Y=\left.\frac{\partial F(w)}{\partial w}\right|_{w=\mathbf{1}_{n}}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n},

which records the influence of every training example on every test query. We write YqY_{q} for its qqth row—the metagradient of query qq—so that recovering YY would allow us to generate counterfactual predictions for all kk queries simultaneously.

2.3 Influence Matrix Estimation

MAGIC recovers row YqY_{q} by differentiating fqf_{q} backward through the entire training trajectory. Thus, recovering all kk rows would require kk replays of training. In this paper, we ask:

Given a budget of only B<kB<k replays, how well can we approximate the influence matrix?

We consider two ways of evaluating the quality of any estimate Y^\widehat{Y} of the full influence matrix under this setting, which emphasize distinct yet equally important aspects of the problem.

Reconstruction. The reconstruction error is given by

‖Y−Y^‖F2=∑q=1k‖Yq−Y^q‖2,\left\|Y-\widehat{Y}\right\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{q=1}^{k}\left\|Y_{q}-\widehat{Y}_{q}\right\|^{2},

which is the standard measure of estimation quality for matrix recovery. This is an appropriate objective in settings where we wish to identify the training data driving model behavior, as is the case with data valuation (Ghorbani and Zou, 2019; Jia et al., 2019).

Attribution. Instead of optimizing directly for the proximity between Y^\widehat{Y} and YY in ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm, we can also measure how well the induced predictions track the behavior of models retrained on the modified data. One objective that captures this notion of counterfactual accuracy is the linear datamodeling score (LDS) (Ilyas et al., 2022). To define the LDS for a given query qq at removal fraction pp, we draw a subset S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] of size n​pnp uniformly at random and write

Δ^q​(S)=−⟨Y^q,𝟏S⟩,Δq​(S)=fq​(𝟏n−𝟏S)−fq​(𝟏n)\widehat{\Delta}_{q}(S)=-\langle\widehat{Y}_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S}\rangle,\qquad\Delta_{q}(S)=f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{S})-f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})

for the predicted change and the true change observed on the model retrained using [n]∖S[n]\setminus S. The LDS for query qq is then given by

LDSq=ρS​(Δ^q​(S),Δq​(S)),\mathrm{LDS}_{q}=\rho_{S}\left(\widehat{\Delta}_{q}(S),\Delta_{q}(S)\right),

where ρS\rho_{S} is the (Spearman) correlation taken over the randomness of SS, and we average the LDS over all the queries. This is an appropriate objective in settings where we wish to predict counterfactual model behaviors under interventions to the training dataset, which transpires in machine unlearning (Guo et al., 2020; Bourtoule et al., 2021) and model interpretability (Koh and Liang, 2017).

3 Mage and Spell

In this section, we present Mage and Spell, our procedures for estimating the influence matrix YY from a budget of B<kB<k calls to the metagradient machinery. The two methods share a conceptually straightforward skeleton of measuring BB well-chosen linear combinations of the rows of YY, and estimating every row by its projection onto the span of the measurements. They differ primarily in the rule selecting the next combination. We present both procedures in Algorithm 1.

3.1 One Replay Can Measure Combinations of Queries

Recall that MAGIC calculates the attribution scores of a single query using reverse-mode differentiation through the training run. However, since differentiation is linear, MAGIC’s computation is not constrained to a single query. To make this precise, let

J=∂θ⁡(w)∂w|w=𝟏n∈ℝp×nJ=\left.\frac{\partial\theta(w)}{\partial w}\right|_{w=\mathbf{1}_{n}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}

denote the Jacobian of the trained model parameters with respect to the nn training weights, whose iith column represents how perturbing the weight of training example ii changes the resulting model parameters. Next, for each query qq, let

vq=∇θϕq​(θ⁡(𝟏n))∈ℝpv_{q}=\nabla_{\theta}\,\phi_{q}(\theta(\mathbf{1}_{n}))\in\mathbb{R}^{p}

denote the gradient of its measurement with respect to the final parameters. By the chain rule, the influence matrix factors as

Y=V⊤​J∈ℝk×n,V=[v1,…,vk]∈ℝp×k.Y=V^{\top}J\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n},\qquad V=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times k}.

Ordinarily, we would recover row YqY_{q} by running REPLAY with vqv_{q} as the input to reverse-mode differentiation. More generally, for any coefficient vector zz, we may instead input the combined query gradient V​zVz, where the same computation returns

(V​z)⊤​J=z⊤​V⊤​J=z⊤​Y∈ℝn.(Vz)^{\top}J=z^{\top}V^{\top}J=z^{\top}Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Therefore, a single replay can measure any chosen linear combination of the rows of YY, and a budget of BB replays allows for BB such chosen combinations.

3.2 A Projection Estimator via Forward-Mode Differentiation

Having laid out the above, we can estimate every row of YY by its projection onto the span of the acquired measurements. Writing

𝒰=span⁡(z1⊤​Y,…,zB⊤​Y)⊆ℝn\mathcal{U}=\operatorname{span}\left(z_{1}^{\top}Y,\ldots,z_{B}^{\top}Y\right)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}

for the subspace derived from BB combinations z1,…,zBz_{1},\ldots,z_{B}, one natural candidate is Y^=Y​Π𝒰\widehat{Y}=Y\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}, where Π𝒰\Pi_{\mathcal{U}} denotes the orthogonal projection onto 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

However, we note that replays themselves can not determine the projection onto 𝒰\mathcal{U}. This is because projecting row YqY_{q} onto 𝒰\mathcal{U} also requires its inner product with every measurement,

⟨Yq,z⊤​Y⟩=vq⊤​J​(z⊤​Y)⊤,\left\langle Y_{q},\,z^{\top}Y\right\rangle=v_{q}^{\top}J\left(z^{\top}Y\right)^{\top},

which involves the unknown row itself. Despite this, we note that the factor J​(z⊤​Y)⊤∈ℝpJ(z^{\top}Y)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is common to every query, and can be calculated using standard forward-mode differentiation, as observed by Gunn (2026). We then pair each replay with an extra forward-mode pass to obtain these inner products. Having this information allows us to update the estimate along the part of the new measurement orthogonal to all previous replays (Golub and Van Loan, 2013), a step we call Extend-Projection in Algorithm 1.

3.3 Reducing the Two Objectives

To design our measurement strategy, we first note that the nature of orthogonal projections paves the way for powerful reductions of both objectives, which we derive below and make use of throughout our procedures.

Reconstruction. For any query qq, we can expand the reconstruction error as

‖Yq−Y^q‖2\displaystyle\left\|Y_{q}-\widehat{Y}_{q}\right\|^{2} =‖Yq‖2−2​⟨Yq,Yq​Π𝒰⟩+‖Yq​Π𝒰‖2\displaystyle=\left\|Y_{q}\right\|^{2}-2\left\langle Y_{q},\,Y_{q}\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right\rangle+\left\|Y_{q}\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right\|^{2}
=‖Yq‖2−2​‖Yq​Π𝒰‖2+‖Yq​Π𝒰‖2\displaystyle=\left\|Y_{q}\right\|^{2}-2\left\|Y_{q}\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right\|^{2}+\left\|Y_{q}\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right\|^{2}
=‖Yq‖2−‖Yq​Π𝒰‖2,\displaystyle=\left\|Y_{q}\right\|^{2}-\left\|Y_{q}\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right\|^{2},

where the second equality holds since Π𝒰\Pi_{\mathcal{U}} is idempotent and symmetric. Summing over the kk queries, we obtain

‖Y−Y^‖F2=‖Y‖F2−‖Y​Π𝒰‖F2,\left\|Y-\widehat{Y}\right\|_{F}^{2}=\|Y\|_{F}^{2}-\left\|Y\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right\|_{F}^{2},

hence minimizing the reconstruction error is equivalent to maximizing the captured energy.

Attribution. To relate the linear datamodeling score to the orthogonal projection, we first reduce the objective through a series of approximations. Fixing a query qq, we can write

LDSq\displaystyle\mathrm{LDS}_{q} =Spearman​-​ρS​(−⟨Y^q,𝟏S⟩,fq​(𝟏n−𝟏S)−fq​(𝟏n))\displaystyle=\mathrm{Spearman}\text{-}\rho_{S}\left(-\langle\widehat{Y}_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S}\rangle,\ f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{S})-f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})\right)
∝∼(1)​Pearson​-​ρS​(−⟨Y^q,𝟏S⟩,fq​(𝟏n−𝟏S)−fq​(𝟏n))\displaystyle\overset{\text{(1)}}{\mathrel{\mathchoice{\hbox{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil\kern-0.6333pt\raise 1.98058pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\propto$}\hfil\cr\hfil\lower 2.23889pt\hbox{$\displaystyle\sim$}\hfil\cr}}}}{\hbox{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil\kern-0.6333pt\raise 1.98058pt\hbox{$\textstyle\propto$}\hfil\cr\hfil\lower 2.23889pt\hbox{$\textstyle\sim$}\hfil\cr}}}}{\hbox{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil\kern-0.54164pt\raise 1.3864pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\propto$}\hfil\cr\hfil\lower 1.56723pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle\sim$}\hfil\cr}}}}{\hbox{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil\kern-0.49164pt\raise 0.99028pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\propto$}\hfil\cr\hfil\lower 1.11945pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\sim$}\hfil\cr}}}}}}\mathrm{Pearson}\text{-}\rho_{S}\left(-\langle\widehat{Y}_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S}\rangle,\ f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{S})-f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n})\right)

Thus, we see that optimizing for the LDS likewise maximizes the captured energy of Y~\widetilde{Y}.

3.4 Selecting the Combinations to Measure

The top-BB right-singular subspace of YY is optimal for reconstruction, and that of Y~\widetilde{Y} is optimal for the attribution surrogate in Equation 2 (Fan, 1949). While the truncated SVD is ordinarily computed from the full matrix, it can also be assembled one direction at a time. To do so, we can probe (i.e., send through replay) the leading eigenvector of the residual Gram matrix,

R=Y⁡(In−Π𝒰)​Y⊤,R=Y\left(I_{n}-\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right)Y^{\top},

where we suppress the iteration index so that 𝒰\mathcal{U} and RR denote the current span and residual. After BB iterations, the span of the measurements recovers the top-BB right-singular subspace (Hotelling, 1933; Golub and Van Loan, 2013).

However, forming the residual Gram matrix would require the rows of YY (or Y~\widetilde{Y} analogously). Instead, Mage and Spell run the iterations using principled stand-ins built from the query gradients and the measurements taken so far, with Mage tracking the truncated SVD of YY and Spell that of its row-normalized counterpart.

Mage. Mage substitutes the query Gram matrix GV=V⊤​VG_{V}=V^{\top}V for RR and probes its leading eigenvectors in order. We also note that

z⊤​GV​z=‖V​z‖2z^{\top}G_{V}z=\|Vz\|^{2}

measures the energy going into replay and z⊤​R​zz^{\top}Rz the unmeasured energy after replay, so the substitution is reasonable whenever JJ preserves the inner products between query gradients.

Spell. To derive the measurements for Spell, we first note that for any probe rr on Y~\widetilde{Y},

r⊤​Y~=(D−1​r)⊤​Y,r^{\top}\widetilde{Y}=(D^{-1}r)^{\top}Y,

which is equivalent to probing z∝D−1​rz\propto D^{-1}r on YY. Since the residual Gram matrix of Y~\widetilde{Y} is

Y~​(In−Π𝒰)​Y~⊤=D−1​R​D−1,\widetilde{Y}\left(I_{n}-\Pi_{\mathcal{U}}\right)\widetilde{Y}^{\top}=D^{-1}RD^{-1},

we can probe vmax​(D−1​R​D−1)v_{\max}(D^{-1}RD^{-1}) on Y~\widetilde{Y}, which amounts to probing z∝D−1​vmax​(D−1​R​D−1)z\propto D^{-1}v_{\max}(D^{-1}RD^{-1}) on YY. Here, both DD and RR are unknown. We can first approximate the entries of DD with

d^q=‖Y^q‖,\widehat{d}_{q}=\|\widehat{Y}_{q}\|,

the length of the measured part of row qq. While d^q\widehat{d}_{q} underestimates ‖Yq‖\|Y_{q}\| due to the unmeasured component, we note that every row is “cut” by the same subspace. Thus, the rankings across queries can stabilize after a few measurements. Since the row norm, and thus its estimate, enters the probe quadratically, any query whose row norm is badly underestimated could commandeer the next probe. To prevent this, we impose a percentile floor

D^=diag⁡(max⁡{d^q,τ}),τ=Q0.1​({d^q:d^q>0}),\widehat{D}=\diag\left(\max\{\widehat{d}_{q},\tau\}\right),\qquad\tau=Q_{0.1}\left(\{\widehat{d}_{q}:\widehat{d}_{q}>0\}\right),

with Q0.1Q_{0.1} the empirical tenth percentile. In practice, we observe that using nearby percentiles (Q0.05Q_{0.05}, Q0.15Q_{0.15}, or Q0.2Q_{0.2}) does not noticeably change the estimate.

To approximate RR, Spell follows Mage’s substitution of GVG_{V}. However, since the maximizer is now taken against the approximation

D^−1​GV​D^−1≈D−1​R​D−1,\widehat{D}^{-1}G_{V}\widehat{D}^{-1}\approx D^{-1}RD^{-1},

where D^−1\widehat{D}^{-1} is updated after every round, the probes no longer come from one fixed eigenbasis. Consequently, the deflation that Mage performs implicitly by probing in order, which removes directions already measured before each round, must now be carried out explicitly.

Since the final estimate depends on any probe zz only through the combined query gradient V​zVz, it follows that deflating zz amounts to removing the part of V​zVz measured by the previous replays, which we can achieve by solving the least squares problem

minβ⁡‖V​z−V​Z​β‖,Z=[z1,…,za−1],\min_{\beta}\left\|Vz-VZ\beta\right\|,\qquad Z=[z_{1},\ldots,z_{a-1}],

with the minimizer given by β=(Z⊤​GV​Z)+​Z⊤​GV​z\beta=(Z^{\top}G_{V}Z)^{+}Z^{\top}G_{V}z. Writing the map z↦z−Z​βz\mapsto z-Z\beta in matrix form, we obtain the Residual-Gram matrix in Algorithm 1,

P=Ik−Z​(Z⊤​GV​Z)+​Z⊤​GV,Gres=P⊤​GV​P.P=I_{k}-Z\left(Z^{\top}G_{V}Z\right)^{+}Z^{\top}G_{V},\qquad G_{\mathrm{res}}=P^{\top}G_{V}P.

Assembling the approximation and residual projection, we arrive at

z∝D^−1​vmax​(D^−1​Gres​D^−1).z\;\propto\;\widehat{D}^{-1}v_{\max}\!\left(\widehat{D}^{-1}G_{\mathrm{res}}\widehat{D}^{-1}\right).

Finally, since the estimates may be unreliable in the initial iterations, we warm up Spell by following Mage for the first a0a_{0} rounds.

4 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate Mage and Spell across two settings. In both settings, we first compute the exact influence matrix YY by running a separate replay for each of the kk queries. For Spell, we set the first a0=max⁡(⌈0.1​B⌉,10)a_{0}=\max(\lceil 0.1B\rceil,10) calls for the warm-up phase in Algorithm 1.

We compare our methods against three baselines at the same budget of BB replays. Random probing replaces Mage’s principal component with a Gaussian combination z∼𝒩⁡(0,Ik)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{k}) of the queries. The first-BB-queries baseline replaces it with the coordinate vector z=eaz=e_{a} for a=1,…,Ba=1,\ldots,B, where these BB queries are chosen by class-balanced round robin on CIFAR-10 and by random permutation on TinyStories.

Principal component analysis (PCA) reconstructs Y^=VB⊤​J\widehat{Y}=V_{B}^{\top}J, where VBV_{B} is the rank-BB SVD of VV, by passing the top-BB principal directions of the query gradients VV directly through replay. We also include two oracle baselines computable only with access to YY, which are the rank-BB singular value decomposition (SVD) of YY, which achieves the smallest reconstruction error at rank BB, and the rank-BB SVD of the row-normalized counterpart of YY.

We evaluate all methods on the two aforementioned objectives in Section 2.3. For reconstruction, we report the relative Frobenius error

‖Y−Y^‖F/‖Y‖F.\left\|Y-\widehat{Y}\right\|_{F}\bigg/\Big\|Y\Big\|_{F}.

For data attribution, we report the linear datamodeling score (LDS). To approximate this quantity for a given test query qq and removal fraction pp, we take the following steps:

  1. 1.

    Draw MM subsets S1,…,SM⊆[n]S_{1},\ldots,S_{M}\subseteq[n] of size n​pnp uniformly at random to be removed from the training set.

  2. 2.

    Retrain the model on each subset [n]∖Sj[n]\setminus S_{j} by setting the weight of every removed example to zero, holding all other training randomness fixed.

  3. 3.

    Record for every test query qq the predicted change Δ^q​(Sj)=−⟨Y^q,𝟏Sj⟩\widehat{\Delta}_{q}(S_{j})=-\langle\widehat{Y}_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S_{j}}\rangle and true change Δq​(Sj)=fq​(𝟏n−𝟏Sj)−fq​(𝟏n)\Delta_{q}(S_{j})=f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}-\mathbf{1}_{S_{j}})-f_{q}(\mathbf{1}_{n}) in the model output function.

  4. 4.

    Compute the Spearman correlation between the predicted and true change over all MM subsets.

Finally, we average the LDS over all kk test queries, which gives

LDS¯=1k​∑q=1kρ⁡([Δ^q​(Sj)]j=1M,[Δq​(Sj)]j=1M)\overline{\mathrm{LDS}}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{q=1}^{k}\rho\left(\Big[\widehat{\Delta}_{q}(S_{j})\Big]_{j=1}^{M},\Big[\Delta_{q}(S_{j})\Big]_{j=1}^{M}\right)

We use M=300M=300 retrained models at two removal fractions of 1%1\% and 5%5\%, and hold the subsets fixed across test queries and methods. We also plot the estimate given by the exact influence matrix −⟨Yq,𝟏Sj⟩-\langle Y_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S_{j}}\rangle as the ceiling (MAGIC).

4.1 ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10

We first consider a ResNet-9 architecture trained on CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky, 2009), where our goal is to attribute the cross-entropy loss on up to k=1000k=1000 held-out test images back to the training data. The model contains 10M parameters and is trained on the full set of 50K training examples (see Appendix B.1 for further details). We then average the results over ten random seeds, where the resulting models attain a mean 89.88%89.88\% test accuracy on the full CIFAR-10 test set. For the figures below, we plot the relative Frobenius error and linear datamodeling score against the number of replays BB over the total number of test queries kk.

We see in Figure 1 that Mage attains the lowest reconstruction error of any implementable method at every budget and query set size. For data attribution, the top panel of Figure 2 shows that Spell consistently outperforms computable alternatives at every size kk once the budget reaches a fifth of the query set size, when 1% of the training data is dropped. Furthermore, as shown in the bottom panel of Figure 2, Spell retains the same advantage when 5% of the training data is dropped.

Table 1 details both metrics at k=500k=500 under the budgets of B=50B=50 and B=100B=100. At B=50B=50, Mage attains a relative Frobenius error of 0.490.49 against 0.530.53 for PCA, 0.620.62 for random probes, and 0.920.92 for the first-BB queries, while Spell obtains an LDS of 0.340.34 against 0.250.25 for random probes, 0.220.22 for the first-BB queries, and 0.150.15 for PCA when dropping 1% of the data.

Finally, in Figure 3, we fix the number of replays at B=50B=50 and vary the size kk of the test query set. We see that both the relative Frobenius error and linear datamodeling score across all methods degrade as kk increases. Nevertheless, both Mage and Spell degrade gracefully and retain their comparative advantages over other methods.

4.2 GPT-2 on TinyStories

For our second domain, we fine-tune a 12-layer GPT-2-style decoder (Radford et al., 2019) on TinyStories (Eldan and Li, 2023). We consider a chunk of 512512 consecutive tokens as a single training example, and the query value is the negative log-likelihood the model assigns to the single token following a held-out chunk of the same length. We fine-tune the model on 20482048 training examples, where our goal is to attribute up to 600600 test queries back to the training data. The model has 92M parameters, and only the fine-tuning stage is attributed starting from a fixed pretrained checkpoint shared across all runs (see Appendix B.2 for further details). We then average the results over four runs, where the fine-tuned models attain a mean 65.04%65.04\% top-1 next-token accuracy on the held-out query corpus.

In Figure 4, we see that Mage attains the lowest reconstruction error of any implementable method at every budget and query set size. For data attribution, the top panel of Figure 5 shows that Spell also outperforms every computable alternative at every kk once the budget reaches a fifth of the query set size, when 1%1\% of the fine-tuning data is dropped. We also see in the bottom panel of Figure 5 that Spell remains performant when 5%5\% of the data is dropped. In greater detail, Table 2 shows that at k=500k=500 with budget B=50B=50, Mage attains a relative Frobenius error of 0.700.70 against 0.710.71 for PCA, 0.820.82 for random probes, and 0.950.95 for the first-BB queries, while Spell obtains an LDS of 0.390.39 against 0.320.32 for random probes, 0.270.27 for the first-BB queries, and 0.230.23 for PCA when dropping 1% of the data.

Finally, in Figure 6, we fix the budget at B=50B=50 and vary the size kk of the test query set, and observe the same degradation as kk increases. Nonetheless, both Mage and Spell maintain their comparative advantages over other methods. While the two scenarios are not directly comparable given that they contain distinct datasets, optimizers, and network architectures, we note that they nevertheless behave alike. Specifically, at the fixed budget B=50B=50, Spell attains 37%37\% of MAGIC’s ceiling on CIFAR-10 and 39%39\% on TinyStories when dropping 1% of the data, and 85%85\% of the performance of rank-BB spherical SVD in both. The ranking among the competitive methods also does not differ across the two domains once B≥0.2​kB\geq 0.2k.

4.3 Reconciling the Two Objectives

Across both settings, Mage attains the lowest reconstruction error whereas Spell attains the highest linear datamodeling score, which may seem conflicting given that Mage recovers the influence matrix almost exactly in terms of the relative Frobenius error. We resolve this apparent contradiction by further examining the geometry of YY in Appendix C.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we cast data attribution at scale as a problem of estimating the influence matrix from a small number of measurements, using the observation that a single replay measures any linear combination of its rows. Next, we introduce Mage and Spell, algorithms tailored to recover the matrix itself and to preserve data attribution fidelity respectively. Across a ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10 and a GPT-2-style decoder on TinyStories, both methods consistently outperform every computable alternative on their targeted objectives. Given that the cost of both procedures is set by the measurement budget rather than by the number of queries, they enable efficient attribution for many queries simultaneously where recovering the exact influence matrix may be computationally prohibitive.

One promising avenue for future work is to investigate whether better selection rules exist, and in particular whether the attribution objective admits a measurement that is optimal in the same way that truncated SVD is optimal for reconstruction, which would help guide the design of practical selection rules at a fixed measurement budget.

Appendix A Proof of the Pearson Correlation Identity

First, we define

H=In−1n​𝟏n​𝟏n⊤,α=p⁡(1−p)​nn−1.H=I_{n}-\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}_{n}\mathbf{1}_{n}^{\top},\qquad\alpha=\frac{p(1-p)n}{n-1}.

For a uniformly random subset SS of size n​pnp, CovS​(𝟏S)=α​H\textrm{Cov}_{S}(\mathbf{1}_{S})=\alpha H, and we can write

Pearson​-​ρS​(−⟨Y^q,𝟏S⟩,−⟨Yq,𝟏S⟩)\displaystyle\mathrm{Pearson}\text{-}\rho_{S}\left(-\langle\widehat{Y}_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S}\rangle,\ -\langle Y_{q},\mathbf{1}_{S}\rangle\right) =Y^q​CovS​(𝟏S)​Yq⊤Y^q​CovS​(𝟏S)​Y^q⊤​Yq​CovS​(𝟏S)​Yq⊤\displaystyle=\frac{\widehat{Y}_{q}\mathrm{Cov}_{S}(\mathbf{1}_{S})Y_{q}^{\top}}{\sqrt{\widehat{Y}_{q}\mathrm{Cov}_{S}(\mathbf{1}_{S})\widehat{Y}_{q}^{\top}}\sqrt{Y_{q}\mathrm{Cov}_{S}(\mathbf{1}_{S})Y_{q}^{\top}}}
=α​Y^q​H​Yq⊤α​Y^q​H​Y^q⊤​α​Yq​H​Yq⊤\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha\widehat{Y}_{q}HY_{q}^{\top}}{\sqrt{\alpha\widehat{Y}_{q}H\widehat{Y}_{q}^{\top}}\sqrt{\alpha Y_{q}HY_{q}^{\top}}}
=Y^q​H​Yq⊤Y^q​H​Y^q⊤​Yq​H​Yq⊤\displaystyle=\frac{\widehat{Y}_{q}HY_{q}^{\top}}{\sqrt{\widehat{Y}_{q}H\widehat{Y}_{q}^{\top}}\sqrt{Y_{q}HY_{q}^{\top}}}
=(Y^q​H)​(Yq​H)⊤‖Y^q​H‖​‖Yq​H‖\displaystyle=\frac{\big(\widehat{Y}_{q}H\big)\big(Y_{q}H\big)^{\top}}{\big\|\widehat{Y}_{q}H\big\|\big\|Y_{q}H\big\|}
=Pearson​-​ρ​(Y^q,Yq),\displaystyle=\mathrm{Pearson}\text{-}\rho(\widehat{Y}_{q},Y_{q}),

where the penultimate equality holds because HH is idempotent and symmetric.

Appendix B Architecture Details

B.1 ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10

Our ResNet-9 consists of eight 3×33\times 3 convolutions, each followed by batch normalization and GELU nonlinearity, and a final linear head. The first layer widens the input image to 80 channels at full resolution, and the second layer widens it to 160 and applies a 2×22\times 2 average pooling. Two more layers at 160 channels form the first residual block. The next two layers widen and downsample twice more, to 320 channels at 8×88\times 8 and then to 640 channels at 4×44\times 4. The last two convolutional layers form a second residual block at 640 channels. A final 4×44\times 4 average pooling reduces each channel to a single value, and a linear head maps the resulting 640-dimensional vector to the ten class logits.

The k=1000k=1000 queries are randomly chosen to ensure balance at 100100 images per class and prefix-nested in kk, so that the k=100k=100 set is the first 100100 rows of the k=1000k=1000 set.

B.2 GPT-2 on TinyStories

Our model is a 12-layer pre-norm transformer decoder of width 768768 with 1212 attention heads of 6464 dimensions. The input is a chunk of 512512 tokens and is mapped through an embedding table and added to a learned position embedding, where we tokenize with a vocabulary of 81928192 entries that contains the 79367936 most frequent words of the pretraining text together with 256256 single-byte fallbacks. Each block applies causal self-attention and a feed-forward network that widens from 768768 to 30723072 through a GELU nonlinearity, preceded by layer normalization and wrapped in a residual connection.

We partition the TinyStories training corpus into chunks of length 512512 and divide them into three splits with no overlap, reserving 896,000896{,}000 chunks for pretraining, 44734473 for fine-tuning, and 10241024 for testing. We attribute on the test split, where each of our four runs fine-tunes on a different draw of n=2048n=2048 chunks from the fine-tuning split.

Appendix C Geometry of the Influence Matrix

In Section 3.3, we have shown that reconstruction and attribution weight queries differently, and have seen in Section 4 that Mage and Spell indeed excel at their respective tasks. Here, we provide some further intuition behind this phenomenon. In particular, we show that for the two scenarios considered in Section 4, the rows of the influence matrix differ by many orders of magnitude in norm.

In Figure 7, we sort the queries using their row norms ‖Yq‖\|Y_{q}\| in decreasing order and plot them along with the share of total energy accumulated thus far. For the ResNet-9 setting considered in Section 4.1 with k=1000k=1000, the norms span 8.68.6 orders of magnitude on CIFAR-10, and the largest quartile of queries holds 99.20%99.20\% of the total energy. For the GPT-2 setting shown in Section 4.2 with k=600k=600, the row norms span 7.47.4 orders of magnitude, where the largest quartile of queries captures 77.14%77.14\% of the total energy on TinyStories.

Since the relative Frobenius error weights each query by the square of its row norm ‖Yq‖2\|Y_{q}\|^{2}, it follows that on CIFAR-10 the error is determined almost entirely by the top quartile. The linear datamodeling score instead averages over every query equally regardless of its norm. Consequently, the same estimate can be scored very differently under the two objectives. To measure this behavior, we consider the mean per-query relative error

1k​∑q=1k‖Yq−Y^q‖/‖Yq‖,\frac{1}{k}\sum_{q=1}^{k}\left\|Y_{q}-\widehat{Y}_{q}\right\|\Big/\Big\|Y_{q}\Big\|,

which normalizes each error by its ground-truth influence. Table 5 shows that Mage attains a relative Frobenius error of 0.00450.0045 on CIFAR-10 at k=1000k=1000 and B=500B=500 against a mean per-query relative error of 0.4470.447. In contrast, Spell attains a balanced performance of 0.4580.458 against 0.5840.584.

To capture a clearer picture of the underlying geometry, we sort the queries by ‖Yq‖\|Y_{q}\| and partition them into quartiles. Table 6 below reports the per-query relative error and the linear datamodeling score within every quartile. Across both scenarios, Mage reconstructs the largest quartile almost exactly but learns little about the smallest quartile, and its attribution quality follows the same pattern. In contrast, Spell remains nearly flat on both measures.

While the smallest quartile may appear unpredictable, the exact influence matrix suggests otherwise, scoring 0.880.88 on the smallest quartile and 0.920.92 on the largest, where Mage attains only 0.350.35 on the smallest against 0.590.59 for Spell on CIFAR-10. This suggests that it could be helpful for practitioners to understand the imbalance in the row norms before deciding on the optimal attribution strategy.

Surprisingly, we also find that the row norms of YY in the scenarios above are nearly perfectly ranked by the norms of the query gradients themselves, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.9990.999 on CIFAR-10 and 0.9960.996 on TinyStories across the same runs. Given that the query gradients are already accessible after training, a practitioner could read off how concentrated a query set is in advance, and decide whether to invoke Mage or Spell before spending any measurement budget. We leave a theoretical justification of why this phenomenon occurs for future investigation.
